blocks.text: X-ray crystallography is a very strong analytical tool used to identify the three-dimensional positions of atoms in a crystalline solid. It is important in materials science, biochemistry and pharmaceutical chemistry because it lets scientists see the structures of materials. X-rays have a very small wavelength, so this radiation can be used to find the positions of electrons and atoms in a molecule or an ionic compound. Solid materials consist of layers or strands of atoms.

When X-rays from a source fall on a crystal, they are diffracted after hitting the atoms at specific angles (Figure 31.4). The diffracted rays make patterns on a screen called diffraction patterns. A diffraction pattern locates the atoms and electrons in a molecule; it can be turned into maps and gives the distances between atoms. Using mathematical models to analyse the pattern, scientists draw a detailed map of atomic positions and bond angles in the crystal, so the complete pattern of atoms and their electron density can be mapped to find the overall structure of the molecule or crystal. Figure 31.5 shows this for naphthalene.

blocks.alt: Left: three rows of red atoms a distance d apart. Two parallel blue X-rays come in at an angle theta and are reflected (purple) from atoms in the first and second rows. Short orange segments mark the extra distance travelled by the lower ray, d sin(theta) going in and d sin(theta) coming out, 2d sin(theta) in all. Right: two fused hexagons of naphthalene with sets of concentric contour circles at each carbon atom.
blocks.caption: X-ray diffraction by layers of atoms, and an electron-density map of naphthalene (original diagram after Figures 31.4 and 31.5).
blocks.long_description: The ray reflected from the lower layer travels 2d sin(theta) further. Where this extra path is a whole number of wavelengths, the reflected rays reinforce and a bright spot appears (n x wavelength = 2d sin(theta), Bragg's law), so the spot angles give the layer spacing d. On the map, contour lines join points of equal electron density, and each peak marks an atom.

blocks.text: The best-known use of X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the determination of the double helix structure of DNA. It is still used to analyse complex biomolecules such as enzymes and proteins. In drug development, designers use it to see how a drug molecule attaches to its target. It is also used to analyse minerals, synthetic crystals and nanomaterials, which helps improve material performance in electronics, optics and construction.
